prompt.problem_text: Route sequencing learned from drivers. A route is a set of stops served by one vehicle that starts and ends at its delivery station (one stop of type `Station`, the others `Dropoff`); it comes with the stops' coordinates and ZONE identifiers (a planning code such as `C-17.3D`; some stops have none), the travel times in seconds between all pairs of stops, and per stop its packages (dimensions, planned service time, sometimes a delivery time window). The task is to propose the ORDER in which the stops are visited so that it is as close as possible to the order the route's own driver used - which is unknown for a new route and must be predicted from how drivers handled other routes of the same station (the history). COST of a route: sequence deviation x edit distance with real penalty per edit between the proposed and the driver's order (travel times normalised per route), as the official scorer of this task computes it; 0 means identical, lower is better. A route for which no valid order is proposed (every stop exactly once, starting at the station) gets a fixed penalty score. The COST OF A RUN is the mean over the routes of its batch. Input of a run: three JSON files of the batch - `new_route_data.json` (station, date, departure time, vehicle capacity, stops), `new_package_data.json`, `new_travel_times.json` - without drivers' orders and without the quality label that the history routes carry. Output: one JSON file {route id: {"proposed": {stop id: position}}} with position 0 for the station.
prompt.solver_text: a pipeline of three parts in `src/`: (1) `scripts/analyze_zone_id_order_main.py` (with `analyze_zone_id_order.py` and `util_zone.py`) builds a MODEL from the history when a version is built - per station, how drivers pass from zone to zone and how zones group into larger units; (2) `scripts/build_TSPLIB.py` turns every route of a batch into a constrained travelling-salesman instance (travel times plus clusters, precedences and neighbourhood relations taken from the model), once per VARIANT listed in `stages.txt`; (3) the solver in C (`solver/`), a tour-improvement local search with penalties for violated constraints, runs on every instance. `stages.txt` gives, per variant, the builder's flags, its share of the solving time and the factor of the rule that picks one variant's tour per route; `solver.par` holds the solver's parameter lines; `scripts/tsplib2json.py` turns tours into stop orders; `tools/tour_length.c` reads a tour's length
prompt.time_text: 240 seconds for a batch of 40 routes on one core (instance building, solving every route once per variant and the conversion all count)
prompt.build_text: `gcc -O3 -w -fcommon -Isolver/include solver/*.c -o prog -lm` and `gcc -O3 -w tools/tour_length.c -o tour_length` in `src/`, after `stages.txt` (1 to 6 lines `name | flags | share | factor`, shares adding up to 1) and `solver.par` (lines `KEY = value`; no file names, no PROBLEM_FILE / SEED / TIME_LIMIT / TOUR_FILE / RUNS) have been checked; then the model: `python3 scripts/analyze_zone_id_order_main.py --r_file <history>/route_data.json --s_file <history>/actual_sequences.json --out_file model.json` (about 1 minutes); then the launcher `solver` is written next to them; `python3 tools/problem.py build src bin` does exactly this in your directory
prompt.io_text: `solver <instance file> <solution file> -t <seconds> -seed <int>`: the launcher writes the batch's three input files; runs `python3 scripts/build_TSPLIB.py --r_file .. --t_file .. --p_file .. --z_file model.json --br_file <history route_data.json> <flags of the variant> <dir>` once per line of `stages.txt` (it must write `<dir>/*.ctsptw` and `<dir>/tsp2ext.json`); runs `prog <parameter file>` once per route and variant, one process at a time, with PROBLEM_FILE, SEED, TIME_LIMIT and TOUR_FILE added to the lines of `solver.par` (the time left for solving is divided among the variants by their shares and equally among the routes, at most 60 s each); keeps per route the tour with the smallest floor(factor x length) as printed by `tour_length`; and runs `python3 scripts/tsplib2json.py --tour_dir .. --tsplib2ext_file .. --out_json ..`. These calls are fixed; everything the called programs do is yours to change
prompt.size_text: `--n` is the number of routes of a batch (the service asks for sizes from {lo} to {hi}).

island_text:
This project is one of three that improve the same solver in parallel, all three on the same training instances. YOURS is the main one: your committed version is the one that will be tested at the end. The two others are scouts: their committed versions are set to yours from time to time (at the start of one of their sessions, when you have committed something new), they are told to stay away from everything you have kept, dropped or are working on, and their role is to give you ideas you have not had. How it works for you:
- `offers/` receives every change a scout commits: one directory per offer, with `change.diff` (the change alone), `after/` (the changed files in full) and `note.md` (what it is and what it measured). The scouts work on the same instances as you, each on its own line of versions (a recent version of yours - or the original solver early on - plus its own commits; `note.md` says which), so an offer's numbers are directly comparable with yours. Whatever you take from an offer goes through your own evaluations and your commit gate like any other change. Say in the evaluation note and in `NOTES.md` which offer it is (`offer S1_v2: ...`), what you decided and why.
- An offer usually needs further work from you before it pays off on your version. It was developed and tuned on the scout's line of versions (`note.md` says what that line was: often an earlier version of yours), while your version may contain newer changes that interact with it: its parameters (rates, periods, sizes, thresholds), the place where it is applied and its share of the run time were chosen for another solver. So treat an offer as a starting point that you optimise, not as a patch that you accept or reject. When an offer does not pass as it is, adapt it to your version - re-tune its key parameters, change when or where it is applied, keep only the part that helps, combine it with what you already have - and measure again. Keep working on an offer until it pays off on your version, or until your measurements show why it cannot (for example: your version already does what it does, or a named interaction with one of your changes cancels it). Leaving an offer is the exception: `NOTES.md` must then give that reason, with every variant you tried and what each measured. A number of attempts is never a reason by itself, and one `probe` whose difference is within the noise is not a reason to leave an offer whose own measurement passed the gate. An offer that passes as it is can still be improved afterwards: look for that too. `offers/INDEX.md` (kept up to date by the service) lists the open offers with what you have measured on each so far and where the scout measured its effect (by instance size: test an offer on the instances it is meant for). Offers whose effect is established in the scout's project (they passed its first gate) are listed first: work on them in that order, before anything else - while one of them is open the service accepts no other declaration. Offers that passed there only through the second gate have an effect within the noise of the measurement: taking one of them up is your choice, and when none of the first group is open they compete for your time with your own ideas on their merits. An offer is closed by a commit of yours that contains it, or - when your measurements show why it cannot pay off on your version - by `python3 tools/ctl.py leave <offer> "<that reason, with the variants you measured>"`.
- `REF_*.md` are briefs of the scouts: what each tried without keeping (do not try it again: it was measured on your instances) and what it is working on now (do not duplicate it; it will arrive as an offer if it succeeds).
- Besides the offers, follow your own ideas.
- Before you start on a new direction (before you write code for it), declare it: `python3 tools/ctl.py claim "<one sentence>"`. The answer gives the record of the other two projects: what each is working on now, what it declared earlier, what it kept, and what it tried and did not keep. If yours is the same idea as anything on that record, or a variant of it, do not start it: think of another and declare that one. (An offer is the exception: it is yours to take up.) One declaration at a time (a new one replaces the old one). The service refuses `probe` and `eval` until you have declared a direction, and again after every commit until you declare the next one. An offer you take up is declared in the same way (`claim "offer S1_v2: ..."`).
island_note: its training instances are the same 10 families of routes as yours
